summary: Year 3 children learn the right angle as a reusable benchmark unit: a quarter turn, the corner of a square, marked with a small square. They build and use a right-angle checker (folded paper / L-shape) to test real corners, classify other angles as less open or more open than a right angle, and compose turns from right angles (two make a half turn, four a complete turn / 360°). Key goal: the right angle's identity is independent of orientation and arm length.
misconceptions: A right angle must be 'upright' like a standard L; a rotated or mirrored one is not recognised as a right angle (orientation dependence)
A right angle drawn with long arms is 'bigger' or 'more than' one with short arms (the arm-length misconception carried over)
Any sharp-looking corner is a right angle — labelling corners by rough appearance rather than testing against the checker
Miscounting right angles in a turn — e.g. two right angles make a full turn, or a half turn returns you to the start

activities.title: Make and use a right-angle checker
steps: Fold a piece of paper (or a paper circle) in half and in half again to make a right-angle tester with a crisp square corner.
Place the checker into real corners around the room and on shapes — a window frame, a book corner, a slice of pizza, an open pair of scissors.
For each corner, decide: does the checker fit flush (a right angle), or is the corner less open / more open than the checker?
Mark each confirmed right angle with a small square symbol.
Deliberately test corners that are tilted off-upright and corners drawn with very long arms, turning the checker to match each corner before reading the fit.
activities.insight: A right angle is one reusable unit of comparison; a corner is a right angle only if it fits the checker exactly, regardless of how it is turned or how long its arms are.

activities.title: Build turns from right angles
steps: Stand facing a chosen landmark (e.g. the window). Predict: how many quarter turns will bring you back to facing exactly the way you started? Say why before turning.
Make the turns one quarter at a time, always turning the same way (e.g. all clockwise), counting one right angle each time and noticing which way you face after each.
Pause after two quarter turns: notice you are facing backwards (a half turn / straight line), not home.
Link to the four compass points and a clock face: a quarter turn is one right angle, two a half turn, three a three-quarter turn, four a full turn (360°).
With a hinge or two geo-strips, open exactly to a right angle and connect: a quarter turn leaves a right angle between the start arm and the finish arm.
activities.insight: Turns are composed of right angles: two right angles make a half turn (facing back), three make a three-quarter turn, and four make a complete turn (360°) back to the start.

activities.title: Sort and classify mixed angles
steps: Look at a set of about five angles laid out in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious upright right angle.
Point to every right angle you can find, testing each with your checker rather than judging by appearance.
Sort the remaining angles into 'less open than a right angle' and 'more open than a right angle'.
Pick one angle you called a right angle and explain how you know — 'it fits my checker / it's a quarter turn / it makes a square corner'.
Order a few angles from least open to most open.
activities.insight: Classifying angles relative to the right-angle benchmark (less / equal / greater) establishes the less-than and greater-than idea informally, ahead of the words acute and obtuse, and relies on testing not appearance.

checkQuestion: Lay out about five angles in mixed orientations: a true right angle tilted off-upright, a true right angle drawn with very long arms, one angle just less open than a right angle, one just more open, and one obvious right angle. Ask: 'Point to every right angle you can find.' Then: 'Pick one you chose and tell me how you know it's a right angle.'
checkAnswer: Selects the true right angles regardless of orientation or arm length (including the tilted one and the long-armed one), leaves out the just-less and just-more ones, and justifies by 'it's a quarter turn / it fits my right-angle checker / it makes a square corner' rather than by how it looks or which way it points.
